papers.title: Internalizing Chain-of-thought into Looped Transformers
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) enables constant-bit-size transformers to perform general-purpose computation through generated tokens (Li and Wang, 2025a), whereas looped transformers carry out the same computation by recurrence in hidden states (latent thought). We construct a family of constant-bit-size looped transformers that interpolates between CoT and latent thought. For a prescribed loop count $L=L(n)$ and a fixed integer $k\ge1$ satisfying $s(n)^{1/k}=\Omega(L)$, our transformer simulates a time-$t(n)$, space-$s(n)$ Turing machine using a context window of $O(s(n)/L)$ and $O(t(n)s(n)^{1/k}/L)$ generated tokens, reducing both resources by a factor of $L$ relative to the corresponding unlooped queue-machine simulation. The construction also holds with softmax attention at constant bit-size, under the finite-precision kernel specified in this paper.

papers.title: Near-Linear Time Maximum Clique in Circular Arc Graphs
papers.abstract: We present a near-linear time algorithm to find a maximum clique in circular arc graphs, the intersection graphs of arcs on the circumference of a circle, answering a 30-year-old open question posed by Bhattacharya and Kaller [J. Algorithms 1997] and Tiskin [CPM 2006]. Our algorithm runs in time $O(n\log^2 n)$, given $n$ circular arcs, where the graph is implicit. Previous approaches take at least quadratic time (unless the implicitly given graph is sparse). To overcome the quadratic barrier, we solve (structured and related) instances of bipartite matching by interpreting them as a single, offline 2D dominance problem, which in turn we model as a shortest paths problem in a planar grid graph. This allows for the final step, which builds on the theory of Monge matrices to obtain sparse representation and efficient distance computations in the grid graph. Additionally, we provide an observation about the structure of circular arc cliques that leads to an algorithm for the weighted version of the problem with a new parameter, the minimum load $d$, which we define as the minimum, over all points on the circle, of the number of arcs containing that point. The algorithm runs in time $O(dn\log\log n + n\log n)$. This is always at least as good as the previous best maximum weight clique algorithm, which runs in time $O(m\log\log n + n\log n)$, where $m$ denotes the number of edges in the implicit intersection graph, because the minimum load satisfies $d \le 2m/n$. [Abstract shortened to meet arXiv's requirements.]

papers.title: Computing faster with a full memory: Catalytic algorithms break time-space lower bounds
papers.abstract: We show that adding "catalytic space" (which starts full and must have its original contents restored at the end of computation) provably speeds up time-and-space-bounded computation. In a natural output model, with $O(\log(n))$ free space and poly($n$) catalytic space, we give algorithms for sorting and the discrete Fourier transform running in time $n^{1+o(1)}$, and an algorithm for matrix multiplication running in time $n^{\omega + o(1)}$. In the same output model, without additional catalytic space, sorting and DFT are known to require time-space product $\Omega(n^2)$, and matrix multiplication is known to require time-space product $\Omega(n^3)$ [Borodin and Cook, 1982] [Beame, 1991] [Yesha, 1984] [Abrahamson, 1991]. This is the first unconditional demonstration that (uniform, non-relativized) catalytic logspace algorithms can outperform their (non-catalytic) logspace counterparts. We give several further results relevant to fast catalytic algorithm design. We observe that many applications of sorting, FFT, and fast matrix multiplication (e.g., kSUM, integer multiplication, and clique counting) can be performed catalytically, giving catalytic logspace algorithms matching (up to subpolynomial factors) the best known unbounded-space runtimes. Furthermore, we give a fast and simple catalytic algorithm for evaluating low-depth threshold circuits, improving the previously known runtime bound from $\widetilde O(|C|4^df)$ to $\widetilde O(|C|2^d)$, where $|C|$ is the total size (i.e. number of wires) of the circuit, $d$ is the depth, and $f$ is the maximum fan-in.

papers.title: Tree Plurality Veto: Voting in Few Rounds with Efficient Communication and Low Metric Distortion
papers.abstract: We consider the metric distortion framework for voting, where $n$ voters and $m$ candidates are embedded in an unknown metric space. A voting rule selects a candidate using only voters' ordinal preferences, and its distortion is the worst-case ratio between the social cost of the selected candidate and the minimum social cost. We study how round complexity trades off against total communication in deterministic voting protocols with low distortion. Deterministic rules can achieve the optimal distortion of $3$ in one round by eliciting complete rankings using $\Theta(nm\log m)$ bits, while a direct sequential implementation of PluralityVeto achieves the same distortion using only $O(n\log m)$ bits but requires $\Theta(n)$ rounds. Our main result is TreePluralityVeto, a deterministic voting protocol that, for every $r\ge 2$, achieves distortion at most $2r-1$ using at most $r$ rounds and $O(n\log m+n s^{1/(r-1)}\log s)$ bits of total communication, where $s = \min\{n, m\}$. The protocol runs PluralityVeto on a hierarchical partition of the voters, collecting restricted rankings in parallel at each level. The branching factor controls the tradeoff between rounds and communication, and a matching-based analysis shows that each level increases the distortion bound by at most $2$.

papers.title: Private Evaluation of High-Dimensional Functions
papers.abstract: We study differentially private black-box evaluation of arbitrary high-dimensional functions. Given a dataset $S$ and query access to a function $f$---whose sensitivity may be unknown or unbounded---the goal is to privately output an approximation to $f(S)$. The black-box evaluator can only query the value of $f$ over a down neighborhood of $S$ (i.e., those subsets of $S$ that are obtained by removing a bounded number of elements from $S$). We design generic black-box evaluators for both pure and approximate differential privacy through a reduction to high-dimensional private quasi-concave optimization (QCO). Our black-box evaluator enjoys a geometric notion of utility. Consider the vectors obtained by applying $f$ on sets in a down neighborhood of $S$. With high probability, the evaluator's output is guaranteed to be in the convex hull of these vectors. Our work generalizes the result of Linder et al. [LRSS25] for real-valued function evaluation to high dimensions. It also recovers the private center-point guarantees of Beimel et al. [BMNS19], with an explicit additive approximation to maximum Tukey depth. We also apply our evaluators to user-level quasi-concave and convex optimization, showing how they can improve upon the sample-and-aggregate baseline of Nissim et al. [NRS07] by replacing the multiplicative data overhead with an additive overhead. Finally, we show that our formulation of high dimensional black-box evaluation and high dimensional private QCO are equivalent up to a factor of the dimension: the hardest private evaluation instances already arise from the cases that $f$ is a (non-private) quasi-concave optimizer.

papers.title: Improved Space Bounds for Promise Graph Coloring in Adversarial Streams
papers.abstract: We study promise graph coloring in one pass insertion-only adversarial streams. We give a randomized algorithm that distinguishes 3-colorable graphs from graphs that are not 6-colorable using $O(n^{3/2}\log(n/\varepsilon)\log n)$ bits of space. This provides a truly subquadratic space algorithm for a constant coloring gap, answering an open problem posed by Assadi, Sundaresan, and Yazdanyar [SODA 2026] for $q=3$. Combining this algorithm with the vertex-sampling lemma of Assadi et al.\ yields, for any $144\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\le Q\le n$, a one-pass decision algorithm distinguishing $3$-colorable graphs from graphs that are not $Q$-colorable using $O((n/Q)^{3/2}\log^5 n)$ bits of space. This improves upon the $\widetilde{O}((n/Q)^2)$ bound achievable via dynamic streaming techniques. Setting $Q=\lceil n^{1/3}\rceil$ yields a semi-streaming decision algorithm, answering the decision version of another open problem posed by Assadi et al. On the negative side, we prove that distinguishing $\chi(G)\le q$ from $\chi(G)\ge(q-1)^2$ requires $\Omega(n^2/q^5)$ bits of space, improving upon the previously established $q^2/4$ threshold using the same space complexity.

papers.title: Enumerating Small Potential Maximal Cliques with Fixed-Parameter Delay
papers.abstract: A potential maximal clique (PMC) of a graph $G$ is a nonempty vertex set that forms a maximal clique in some minimal triangulation of $G$. Listing the PMCs of a graph is a key step in exact algorithms for computing treewidth, minimum fill-in, and related graph parameters. We present a deterministic algorithm that enumerates all PMCs of cardinality at most $k$ in an $n$-vertex graph $G$, without repetition, with delay $2^{O(k^3)}n^4\log n$. This bound also covers the preprocessing time before the first output, the time from the last output to termination, and the total running time when no such PMC exists. At the core of our enumeration algorithm is a procedure that solves the following constrained search problem within the same time bound: given sets of required and excluded vertices $I,O\subseteq V(G)$, find a PMC $\Omega$ of size at most $k$ satisfying $I\subseteq\Omega$ and $\Omega\cap O=\emptyset$, or determine that none exists. Our enumeration algorithm directly supports these inclusion and exclusion constraints as well. Our approach builds on the \emph{recursive understanding} technique of Chitnis et al.~\cite{chitnis2016} and the reduction to unbreakable graphs of Lokshtanov et al.~\cite{lokshtanov2018}. A graph is $(q,k)$-unbreakable if no removal of at most $k$ vertices leaves two disjoint unions of connected components that each contain more than $q$ vertices. We first solve constrained PMC search on $(q,k)$-unbreakable graphs, and then apply this procedure to replace separated subgraphs with graphs of size $2^{O(k^2)}$ that preserve the existence of a constrained solution for every graph attached along the shared boundary.

papers.title: Navigable Graphs for Low-Dimensional Hyperbolic Spaces
papers.abstract: A directed graph on a point set $P$ in a metric space $(X,d)$ is navigable if for every ordered pair of distinct points $s,t \in P$, $s$ has an out-neighbor $v$ with $d(v,t) < d(s,t)$, so greedy routing always reaches the destination. Existing work on sparse navigable graphs mostly assumes bounded doubling dimensions. In this paper, we show that constant-dimensional hyperbolic spaces that do not have bounded doubling dimension also admit sparse navigable graphs. Specifically, for an $n$-point set in $\mathbb H^k$ with a constant $k$, we construct a navigable graph of size $O_k(n)$ with Steiner points, where each node has constant out-degree. We also show that Steiner points can be removed: every $n$-point set in $\mathbb H^k$ admits a navigable graph on the input points alone with $O_k(n)$ edges, though a single vertex may have out-degree $\Omega(n)$. Furthermore, with a refined construction with $O_k(n\log n)$ edges and an accompanying greedy routing algorithm, we can obtain routing paths of expected $O(\log ^2 n)$ in both settings with or without Steiner points. With Steiner points, the maximum out-degree is bounded by $O_k(\log n)$. We complement these upper bounds with matching lower bound results. In the hyperbolic plane, there are point sets for which every navigable graph requires maximum out-degree $\Omega(n)$, so the maximum linear out-degree above is unavoidable and constant out-degree is only possible with Steiner points. Next, we show that for every constant $\alpha>1$, an $\alpha$-navigable graph may require $\Omega(n^2)$ edges, which rules out the standard route of using $\alpha$-navigability to obtain greedy paths of bounded hops. Last, once the dimension $k$ reaches $\Omega(\log n)$, there are point sets for which every navigable graph may require $n^{3/2-o(1)}$ edges, matching the upper bounds for general metrics.

papers.title: Approximating Independent Sets Using Additive Combinatorics
papers.abstract: We give a deterministic quasi-polynomial time algorithm for approximating the largest independent set in a graph. We show that if an $N$-vertex graph contains an independent set of size $2^{-t} N$, then we can find an independent set of size $2^t$ in quasi-polynomial time, for all $t$ up to a constant factor of $(\log N)^{1/3}$. This gives an approximation factor of $N / \exp((\log N)^{1/3})$, which has the same shape as known hardness results for quasi-polynomial time algorithms, up to a different exponent of the logarithm. The algorithm builds on a structural principle: a graph containing a large independent set must also contain a large sparse structured set, and such a set can be found efficiently. A greedy algorithm then extracts an independent set from it. Our proof draws on tools in additive combinatorics, in particular spreadness and sifting, to obtain the combinatorial structural results. We then convert these to efficient algorithms using pseudo-marginals obtained by semidefinite programming.

papers.title: Subexponential Algorithms for Total Search Problems in the Dense Pigeonhole Regime
papers.abstract: The class $\mathsf{PPP}$ captures fundamental total search problems, for which a solution is guaranteed to exist by the pigeonhole principle and the main challenge is to find it. We ask whether problems in this class admit significantly faster algorithms in the \emph{dense regime}. More concretly, we study \emph{binary collision Short Integer Solution} (SIS): given a matrix $A\in\mathbb{Z}_q^{n\times m}$ with $m>n\log q$, the goal is to find distinct $\underline{\mathbf{x}},\underline{\mathbf{y}}\in\{0,1\}^m$ with $A\underline{\mathbf{x}}=A\underline{\mathbf{y}}\pmod q$. Brute-force enumeration can be used to find a collision in $q^{\mathcal{O}(n)} \operatorname{poly}(|I|)$ time, and no significantly faster algorithm for that problem is known. We present an algorithm running in time $q^{o(n)}\cdot\operatorname{poly}(|I|)$ whenever the density parameter $\delta:= m/(n\log q)$ is $\omega(1)$.\footnote{All logarithms are in base $2$, and $|I|$ is the binary input length.} Building on reductions of Sotiraki et al.~(FOCS~2018), we obtain corresponding algorithms for dense variants of weak constrained SIS, Equal Vector Sums, Minkowski, and Blichfeldt. Our algorithm adapts techniques of Bhati et al.~(FOCS~2026), who gave a subexponential algorithm for Equal Sums in the dense regime and proved a tight conditional lower bound. Their conditional lower bound easily transfers to SIS and shows that the running time of our algorithms is essentially optimal.

papers.title: Orienting mixed graphs for reachability pairs: When the all pairs setting is easier than the general one
papers.abstract: Given a mixed graph $G$ and an ordered pair $(u,v)$ of vertices in $V(G)$, we say that an orientation $\vec{G}$ of $G$ satisfies $(u,v)$ if $v$ is reachable from $u$ in $\vec{G}$. We consider problems in which we seek orientations that satisfy a maximum number of pairs. We distinguish between two different problems. In the most general problem called Fixed Pairs Maximum Mixed Reachability Orientation (FPRO), a multiset $P$ of ordered pairs of vertices in $V(G)$ comes with the input. In the more restricted problem All Pairs Maximum Mixed Reachability Orientation (APRO), $P$ contains exactly one copy of every ordered pair of distinct vertices in $V(G)$. We compare the computational complexity of FPRO and APRO in two ways: First, we show that both FPRO and APRO behave similarly when it comes to approximation. Namely, they both admit an asymptotic approximation, but are unlikely to admit a constant factor approximation. Then, we consider the parameterization with respect to the treewidth of the underlying graph of the input mixed graph. We show that here the complexities of FPRO and APRO differ significantly. While it is well-known that FPRO is NP-hard even when this parameter is 1, we show that APRO is XP with respect to this parameter. On the other hand, we give a $W[1]$-hardness result for APRO.

papers.title: Nearly Tight Lower Bound for Range Minimum Query via Probe-by-Probe Information Accounting
papers.abstract: We prove a nearly tight lower bound for succinct Range Minimum Query (RMQ) on an array of $n$ distinct integers. A query returns the position of the smallest entry in a specified subarray. For word size $\Theta(\log n)$, any cell-probe data structure answering queries in time $t$ requires $2n-1.5\log n+n/(\log n)^{O(t\log^2 t)}$ bits of space. This improves the exponent $O(t^2\log^2 t)$ in the lower bound of Liu and Yu (STOC 2020), leaving only a polylogarithmic gap in query time from the known upper bound across the redundancy range. The key ingredient is probe-by-probe information accounting. The previous analysis measures useful information at an "average" memory-access round of an adaptive query algorithm. For RMQ, the informative queries are database-dependent and unevenly distributed, making the conversion from this information to query savings lose a factor of $t$. We account for information across all memory accesses using an entropy telescoping argument. This gives a stronger progress bound within the existing published-bit round-elimination framework. The resulting viewpoint suggests a way to address similar averaging losses in other succinct lower bounds, although applications beyond RMQ remain open.

papers.title: Bonsai: A class of effective methods for independent sampling of graph partitions
papers.abstract: We develop effective methods for constructing an ensemble of district plans via independent sampling from a reasonable probability distribution on the space of graph partitions. We compare the performance of our algorithms to that of standard Markov Chain based algorithms in the context of grid graphs and state congressional and legislative maps. For the case of perfect population balance between districts, we provide an explicit description of the distribution from which our method samples.

papers.title: $\Omega((\log n/\log\log n)^2)$ Lower Bounds for Dynamic Graph Problems
papers.abstract: We prove an $\Omega((\log n/\log\log n)^2)$ unconditional lower bound on the maximum of the update time and the query time for P\u{a}tra\c{s}cu's multiphase problem [STOC 2010] with Disjointness, in its insert-only form. Through his reductions, we obtain the same lower bound for dynamic data structures supporting reachability queries in $n$-node directed acyclic graphs under edge insertions, improving the $\widetilde{\Omega}(\log^{3/2} n)$ lower bound of Larsen and Yu [SICOMP 2025], and matching the strongest lower bound known for any dynamic problem. The same bound holds for many other dynamic problems: in directed graphs, for incremental $s$-$t$ reachability, strong connectivity and cycle detection; in undirected graphs, for incremental shortest paths, subgraph connectivity and triangle detection; and for dynamic set disjointness, range mode, and Langerman's, Pagh's and Erickson's problems. Ko [FOCS 2026] recently proved this bound for a variant of the multiphase problem with Inner Product in place of Disjointness, via a 2.5-round multiphase communication game; we bring this framework to the original problem. Our main technical contribution is to show that verification in this game makes a one-sided corruption bound suffice in place of discrepancy, which Disjointness lacks.

papers.title: Undirected Network Coding and Faster External-Memory Integer Sorting
papers.abstract: Network coding allows intermediate nodes to combine messages. Fractional routing instead splits each message among source-destination paths and forwards its parts without combining different messages. For undirected networks carrying independent messages between multiple source-destination pairs, the multiple-unicast conjecture asserts that the two methods achieve the same combinations of message rates. We give a finite counterexample and use its linear structure to accelerate external-memory integer sorting, addressing the question of whether integer operations can beat the comparison-sorting input/output (I/O) bound posed by Aggarwal and Vitter in 1988. We give a deterministic sorting algorithm: for $N$ integers of $\Theta(\log N)$ bits, a memory holding $M$ integers, and block transfers of $B$ integers, where $2B\le M\le N$, the number of block transfers is $O\!\left(\frac{N}{B}\left[1+\frac{\log N}{(\log(M/B))^{1-\varepsilon}(\log M)^\varepsilon}\right]\right)$, where $\varepsilon=1.5\times10^{-5}$ is an absolute constant. In some parameter ranges, this bound is asymptotically smaller than the classical comparison-sorting bound. Under the external-memory model specified in this paper, we have formally verified the algorithm's correctness and I/O complexity bound in Lean.

papers.title: Constant-Factor Local Approximation for Bipartite Densest Subgraph
papers.abstract: Given a vertex $v$ in a large bipartite graph $G$, can one quickly find a small densely connected region near $v$? This is the algorithmic core of many fraud detection, community detection, and recommender systems. One would like a local algorithm, i.e., an algorithm that probes $G$ in only a small number of locations to find such a region. Our main contribution is the first constant-factor local approximation, independent of the maximum degree of the graph, for the classical notion of bipartite density: if the sides of a bipartite subgraph are $S$ and $T$, its density is $d(S,T):=e(S,T)/\sqrt{|S||T|}$, where $e(S,T)$ is the number of edges between $S$ and $T$. We consider cohesive dense subgraphs, since every dense subgraph contains a cohesive core of at least the same density. For such a cohesive dense subgraph $S\mathbin{\dot\cup}T$ with at most $k$ vertices per side, our algorithm, starting from any vertex in $S\mathbin{\dot\cup}T$, uses $O_\epsilon(k^{4+\epsilon})$ neighbor queries to find a subgraph $X\mathbin{\dot\cup}Y$ of density $\Omega_\epsilon(d(S,T))$ on $O_\epsilon(k^{2+\epsilon})$ vertices, for every fixed $\epsilon>0$. Our result improves upon the result of Andersen (2010), whose approximation guarantee depends logarithmically on the maximum degree. We complement our positive result with information-theoretic and computational limitations showing that the quadratic dependence on $k$ in the output size is essentially unavoidable for constant-factor approximation. Our main technical innovation is an adaptation of the Lov\'asz-Simonovits curve to the bipartite density problem, based on weak-$\ell_p$ norm bounds.

papers.title: Implicit Hitting Set Enumeration for Power Dominating Sets
papers.abstract: The Transversal Hypergraph problem asks to enumerate (list) all inclusion-minimal hitting sets of a hypergraph. It usually assumes that the input is completely known and does not change over the course of the enumeration. In many applications, the underlying hypergraph is too large or expensive to compute. This motivated the implicit hitting set framework [Chandrasekaran, Karp, Moreno-Centeno, and Vempala, SODA 2011] for the corresponding optimization problem of finding a smallest hitting set. Access to the input is given by an oracle that either confirms that a query set $S$ is a hitting set, or reveals a new hyperedge disjoint from $S$. We adapt this framework to enumeration. We show for a general class of algorithms that they are able to find all hitting sets when given access to such an oracle, even if the hypergraph is a priori unknown. We also prove that the current fastest Transversal Hypergraph algorithm, Minimal-to-Maximal Conversion Search by Murakami and Uno [DAM 2014], belongs to this class. We then engineer an implicit hitting set algorithm for the enumeration of minimal power dominating sets in graphs. A power dominating set is a selection of vertices that "observe" all vertices by exhaustively applying two rules: if a vertex is dominated by the selection, it becomes observed; and if an observed vertex has a unique unobserved neighbor, this neighbor becomes observed as well. An experimental evaluation on a collection of power grid instances from the literature shows that our approach achieves very high throughput rates.

papers.title: Batch range mode in O(n+Q)^1.395
papers.abstract: We give a deterministic worst-case algorithm for exact Batched Range Mode on an arbitrary array of length n and a batch of Q intervals. The algorithm returns the mode frequency and the smallest mode identifier for each query in time (n+Q)^(tau+o(1)), where tau = 5 - sqrt(13) = 1.394448724536... . The algorithm combines virtual occurrence windows and block-boundary snapping with a query-restricted min-plus product whose first operand is column-monotone and whose second operand is row-monotone. A deterministic modular verifier uses geometric and query potentials to bound the same active regions; false modular matches are corrected by offline orthogonal range updates. The final analysis uses the sharper rectangular exponent curve of Uznanski (2026), together with exact rational parameter balancing and a transfer to prime fields. The analysis covers every frequency scale and arbitrary batch sizes. Exact frequencies and the smallest mode identifiers are recovered without increasing the exponent.

papers.title: Vertex Ordering for Exact Triangle Listing: Concave Geometry and Certified Rounding
papers.abstract: Exact forward triangle listers orient each edge of a graph by a vertex order. The order does not change the output, but it changes the work. For the adaptive lister, which scans the smaller of the two forward neighborhoods, the number of candidate tests is a known sum of minima of forward degrees, but how to optimize it had not been characterized. We show that this work is a concave function of the forward degrees, so choosing an order is concave minimization over the orientation polytope, whose vertices are the forward-degree vectors of orders. A single sort therefore rounds any point of the polytope, including the out-degree vector of any orientation, to an order with no more work, with a computable lower bound on the improvement. Minimizing the work is nevertheless NP-hard and APX-hard on triangle-free graphs of maximum degree three, and under the Unique Games Conjecture it has no polynomial-time constant-factor approximation. We also analyze logistic score relaxations and the large-graph limit of degree-based orders; on random cubic graphs, the expected work of every degree-based order is asymptotically at least $2.43$ times the expected optimum. Tangent refinement followed by iterated local search reduces the work by \HeldTIKMean\% on average on nine held-out networks fixed by a pre-registered protocol, and by \NSFrozenTILSMean\% in a supplementary rescoring, specified in advance, against a stronger reference that adds the published Neigh local search. The gains are in candidate tests; we observe no reproducible wall-clock speedup.

papers.title: A Combinatorial $(1/2-\varepsilon)$-Approximation for $k$-Submodular Maximization under Multiple Knapsacks
papers.abstract: We give a randomized combinatorial \((1/2 - \varepsilon)\)-approximation for nonnegative non-monotone \(k\)-submodular maximization under a fixed number \(d\) of knapsack constraints, for \(k \ge 2 \). The algorithm selects whole elements and follows the proportional top-2 rule of Chen et al. \cite{chen2026}: it samples from the two labels with the largest marginal gains, with probabilities proportional to the positive parts of these gains. Extending their single-knapsack Bellman analysis, we construct a common resource potential and associated resource weights, with potential losses charged to greedy gains. Since these weights depend on the unknown optimum, we discretize their defining coefficients and enumerate monotone guesses over phases determined by resource consumption. This yields an algorithm using at most $\mathcal{A}(d,\varepsilon)(nk+1)^{H+2}$ value queries, where $n$ is the number of elements, $\mathcal{A}(d,\varepsilon)$ depends only on $d$ and $\varepsilon$, and $H=O(d \log(2d) / \varepsilon^2)$. The approximation ratio can be made arbitrarily close to the optimal oracle threshold for \( k=2 \) and is asymptotically tight as \(k \to \infty\).

papers.title: Tight weighted paging with delay via mirror descent
papers.abstract: We give an O(log k)-competitive randomized algorithm for weighted paging with delay. This improves upon the O(log k log n)-competitive algorithm of Gupta, Kumar, and Panigrahi (STOC 2020, SICOMP 2022) by removing the dependence on the number n of pages. Without delay, the optimal competitive ratio of randomized algorithms is Theta(log k), and since the lower bound carries over, our bound is tight. Our algorithm is fractional and combines mirror descent, used by Bubeck et al. (STOC 2018) for weighted paging without delay, with preemptive service, introduced by Azar et al. (STOC 2017) for online service with delay: when a request is served, an increase in the mirror descent potential is offset by preemptive service to other pending requests, with a budget derived from the mirror descent path. To obtain a randomized algorithm, we use the online rounding of Bansal, Buchbinder, and Naor (FOCS 2007) from classical paging.

papers.title: Mean-only Prophet Inequalities
papers.abstract: We study mean-based algorithms for single-choice prophet inequalities: the algorithm knows the number of variables and the mean of their maximum, but not their distributions. For arbitrary independent variables in a fixed order, we can already achieve the optimal $1/2$ competitive ratio using only this mean. For i.i.d. variables and prophet secretary, however, we previously knew only a $1-1/e$ guarantee, which is far away from the ratios with full distribution information. We improve the guarantees in both settings using a simple and natural algorithm: we fix a continuous decreasing threshold function that depends only on the mean and accept the first variable exceeding its threshold. For i.i.d. variables, we prove a $0.7419$ competitive ratio. For the prophet secretary, we prove a $0.6902$ competitive ratio.

papers.title: Simplified and Faster Algorithms for the Directed Single/Dual-Failure Replacement Paths via Modulo-Layer Hitting Sets
papers.abstract: We study the replacement paths problem in unweighted directed graphs with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges under one or two edge failures. We give simpler and faster algorithms for both settings. Both algorithms are based on a new technique, which we call \emph{modulo-layer hitting sets}. For the single-failure setting, we obtain a simple deterministic combinatorial algorithm running in $O(m\sqrt{n})$ time, which is nearly optimal under the combinatorial Boolean Matrix Multiplication (BMM) conjecture. In addition to removing the logarithmic overhead of the deterministic $\tilde{O}(m\sqrt{n})$-time algorithm of Alon, Chechik, and Cohen~[ICALP'19], our algorithm admits a much simpler implementation and analysis. For the dual-failure setting, we obtain a randomized combinatorial algorithm running in $\tilde{O}(n^{3-1/4})$ time. This improves upon the previous $\tilde{O}(n^{3-1/18})$-time combinatorial algorithm of Chechik and Zhang~[ICALP'24].

papers.title: Algorithms for Connected Multicuts of Weighted Trees
papers.abstract: In the \emph{connected multicut problem for weighted trees}, the instance is an edge-weighted tree $T = (V,E,\omega)$, a set of terminals $\Gamma\subseteq V$, and a set of pairwise ``conflicts'' between these terminals represented by edges of a conflict graph $\mathcal{C} = (\Gamma,\mathcal{F})$. A \emph{connected multicut} for this instance is a partition $\mathcal{M}$ of the vertex set $V$ into subsets called the \emph{components of $\mathcal{M}$}, where each component induces a subtree of $T$, contains at least one terminal, but does not contain any conflicting terminal pair. Two cost functions for multicuts are considered: in the min-sum variant, we minimize the total weight of the edges between different components of $\mathcal{M}$, and in the min-max variant, we minimize the maximum, over all components, of the total weight of edges leaving the component. In the first part of the paper, we focus on algorithms for the min-max variant, for which we give a $2$-approximation algorithm for the unweighted case, a $(2+\epsilon)$-approximation algorithm for the general case, and a mildly exponential exact algorithm for the unweighted case. In the second part of the paper, we study algorithms that take advantage of the structure of the conflict graph. We first give a polynomial-time exact algorithm for the min-max variant when $\mathcal{C}$ is a clique (the variant referred to in the literature as the \emph{multiway cut}). Next, we generalize this result by providing polynomial-time exact algorithms, for both variants, for instances whose conflict graph has constant \emph{split complexity} --- a new parameter that refines the concept of neighborhood diversity previously studied in the context of parameterized complexity. This unifies and generalizes previous results for the min-sum variant when conflict graphs are complete multipartite graphs or unions of cliques.

papers.title: No Escape from the Quadratic Barrier: Adaptive Attacks on Linear $\ell_2$ Sketches
papers.abstract: Linear sketches estimate properties of high-dimensional inputs from a fixed low-dimensional projection. At constant accuracy, randomized Euclidean-norm sketches, notably the Johnson-Lindenstrauss transform, support exponentially many nonadaptive queries in sketch dimension $k$. For adaptive black-box queries, known privacy-based defenses guarantee $\widetilde{\Omega}(k^2)$ and it remained open whether stronger guarantees were possible. Prior attacks used more queries, restricted the responder, or provided weaker failure guarantees. We show that the quadratic guarantee is optimal up to logarithmic factors, even with a computationally unbounded responder that knows the matrix, attack algorithm, history, and query distributions and may change its randomized rule after every query. For every fixed hidden $A\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times n}$ with $n>40k$ and target accuracy $\alpha \in (0,1]$, our black-box attack uses $O(k+\alpha^2k^2\log(2+\alpha^2k))$ queries in $\widetilde{O}(1+\alpha^2k)$ adaptive rounds to force, with constant probability, a round in which a constant fraction of answers have $\Omega(\alpha)$ relative error. Our results clarify the limits of defending a fixed compressive linear representation by adapting the prediction rule.

papers.title: Strategy recovery for Mean-Payoff Games is as hard as solving them from scratch
papers.abstract: Mean-Payoff Games (MPGs) form an interesting family of deterministic, infinite-duration, zero-sum, turn-based games played by two players on a finite weighted directed graph. The goal of the players is to minimize, respectively maximize, the $\textit{limiting average}$ of the costs of the edges on an infinite path constructed by the two players. The complexity of solving MPGs is a long-standing open question. The decision problem associated with these games is known to be in $\text{NP}\cap \text{co-NP}$, and even $\text{UP}\cap \text{co-UP}$, yet the problem is not known to be in $\text{P}$. This is one of the simplest combinatorial problems with such a status. A full solution of an MPG gives the $\textit{value}$ of each vertex of the game, along with a pair of $\textit{optimal strategies}$ for the two players. (Each player has a succinct $\textit{positional}$ optimal strategy.) The problem of finding optimal strategies for the players given the values of all vertices is known as the $\textit{strategy recovery}$ problem. We describe a simple reduction from the problem of solving MPGs to the strategy recovery problem for MPGs. This shows that the strategy recovery problem for MPGs is essentially as hard as solving MPGs from scratch, i.e., without knowing the values. The reduction uses simple $\textit{game transformations}$ and simple $\textit{self-reducibility}$ and $\textit{peeling}$ arguments. This answers a question of Andersson and Miltersen. Mamino obtained a similar result for $\textit{stochastic}$ games with a limiting average objective, but his technique does not extend to deterministic games such as MPGs. We go one step further and show that finding an optimal strategy for one of the players of an MPG remains hard even if an optimal strategy of the second player, and hence all the values, are known.

papers.title: A Faster Strongly Polynomial Time Algorithm for Submodular Function Minimization
papers.abstract: We give a strongly polynomial time algorithm for submodular function minimization with overall running time $\widetilde{O}(n^{2}\mathsf{EO}+n^{3})$ time, where $\mathsf{EO}$ is the running time of a single evaluation of the function. Our algorithm improves upon the previously fastest strongly polynomial algorithms of Lee et al. (FOCS 2015), Dadush et al. (SODA 2018), and Jiang et al. (SODA 2024) that run in time $\widetilde{O}(n^{3}\mathsf{EO}+n^{4})$. Similarly to prior works, our work combines a cutting plane algorithm with the combinatorial arc-finding framework of Fleischer et al. (JACM 2001). We achieve our faster running time by developing an algorithm that runs the cutting plane method end to end, without restarting after discovering arcs and contracting strongly connected components.

papers.title: Range Queries for Permutation Pattern Matching: Separations, Equivalences, and Applications
papers.abstract: The problem of Permutation Pattern Matching (PPM) asks, given a permutation $\pi:[n]\to[n]$, viewed as the point set $P=\{(i,\pi(i)):i\in[n]\}$, and a pattern $\sigma$ of small length $k$, whether $P$ contains an order-isomorphic copy of $\sigma$. The PPM problem and its (exact and approximate) counting variants have been studied extensively in the literature. We consider a preprocessing-query version: after preprocessing $P$, one must determine whether a query $P'\subseteq P$ contains $\sigma$, where $P'$ is obtained by intersecting $P$ with a geometric shape (e.g., an axis-aligned rectangle or $k$ such rectangles). This naturally generalizes the classical range query problem in computational geometry, which corresponds to the case $|\sigma|=1$. We extend the study of this problem from patterns of length $2$ to patterns of length $3$ (and in some cases beyond), and prove new fine-grained equivalences, separations, and applications: (1) Single rectangle: For all patterns of length $3$, detection can be done with $\tilde{O}(n)$ preprocessing and $\tilde{O}(1)$ query time. The proof goes through a new tool of independent interest: reductions from rectangle queries to a simpler family of slab queries. (2) Multiple rectangles: For $\sigma=132$, detection is equivalent to the online set disjointness problem; we also show connections to online $k$-set disjointness. To our knowledge, this is the first equivalence between a PPM-type problem and online set disjointness, a problem playing a fundamental role in fine-grained complexity. (3) Counting: As applications, we obtain an $O(n^{1.725})$ time algorithm for exact counting of $5$-patterns based on the rectangle-to-slab reduction, improving upon [Beniamini and Lavee, ICALP 2025], and an $\tilde{O}(n^{7/4})$ approximate counting algorithm for $6$-patterns, the first to break the $O(n^2)$ barrier for $6$-patterns.

papers.title: Degree Stability of Parallel Greedy Matching in Random Graphs
papers.abstract: We study a natural synchronous greedy matching process in Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi random graphs $\mathbb{G}(n,p)$ and give a rigorous analysis of this parallel stochastic dynamics. The process evolves as follows: in each round, every unmatched vertex proposes to a uniformly random neighbour, and mutually proposing pairs are matched and removed from the graph, after which the process repeats on the residual graph. We consider the density regime $p=\Theta(\log^{1+\epsilon} n/n)$ for any constant $\epsilon>0$, which lies just above the threshold for the existence of a perfect matching. We show that, with high probability, for $\Theta(\log^{1+\epsilon} n)$ rounds, every unmatched vertex keeps a constant fraction of its initial degree in the residual graph, simultaneously for all vertices and all rounds. By then, the process has matched a constant fraction of the vertices. Our analysis tracks fine-grained invariants that control the evolution of individual vertex degrees, rather than directly tracking the global degree distribution. At the local level, we analyze the per-round degree loss of a vertex via a neighbourhood-exposure martingale. We show that structural sparsity of $\mathbb{G}(n,p)$ yields $O(1)$ variance and thus the per-round degree loss is strongly concentrated around its conditional expectation. At the global level, these local concentration bounds control the increments of a martingale tracking cumulative degree loss over many rounds, allowing us to show that vertex degrees remain stable for $\Omega(\log^{1+\epsilon} n)$ rounds.

papers.title: Searching subgraphs
papers.abstract: We consider graph search models, in which an invisible, omniscient and fast intruder can hide anywhere in the graph, and the goal is to design a \emph{search strategy} composed of a sequence of movements of \emph{searchers} that guarantees the capture of the intruder regardless of its actions. Our point of departure is the connected search model in which the cleared subgraph is always connected during the search process. In this paper, we initiate the study of the subgraph searching problems which arise from the following question: what happens if the number of searchers available is not sufficient to clear a given graph $G$? We propose an approach in which one wants to clear in a connected way as large subgraph as possible with the given $k$ searchers. In this context we study two problems: one problem, called the \emph{subgraph search}, is to find the maximum-sized subgraph whose search number is at most $k$, and the other one, called the \emph{protected subgraph search}, is to perform a partial search on $G$ leading to as many cleared edges as possible. Informally speaking, the difference lies in the fact that in the latter a recontamination may come from an edge never to be cleared and hence the partial search strategy needs to avoid such recontaminations. Having proved that both problems are computationally hard in general, we give efficient algorithms for $n$-vertex trees: an $\bigo(\min\{kn, n \log n\})$ time algorithm for the subgraph search and an $\bigo(\min\{2^{6k}kn, n^{8.571} \log n\})$ time algorithm for the protected subgraph search.
